theory.title: Understanding Robot Framework Test Cases and the Log Keyword
theory.content:
Test Cases: Your First Steps

Robot Framework uses a keyword-driven approach. Think of keywords as building blocks—each one does something specific, and you combine them to create test workflows.

The Basic Structure

Every Robot Framework file has sections marked by ***. Here's your first test:

*** Test Cases *** My Test Name Keyword Argument1 Argument2 Another Keyword Argument
⚠️ Spacing Rules (Critical!)
  • Test names start at the left (no indentation)
  • Keywords must be indented with exactly 4 spaces
  • Separate keywords and arguments with 4 spaces
  • This isn't optional—wrong spacing = errors
The Log Keyword

Log is your debugging friend. It prints messages to the test log, helping you see what's happening during execution.

Log Hello Robot Framework!
💡 Why Use Log?
  • Debugging: See variable values as tests run
  • Verification: Confirm code paths execute
  • Documentation: Add runtime notes to reports
What Happens When You Run This?
  1. Robot Framework finds the *** Test Cases *** section
  2. It identifies your test case "My First Test"
  3. It executes each indented keyword line-by-line
  4. The Log keyword outputs to log.html
  5. If all keywords succeed, the test passes ✅

Master this pattern now—you'll use it for every test you ever write. The spacing rules apply to all 1000+ Robot Framework keywords.
learningObjectives: Understand the structure of a Robot Framework test case
Master the 4-space indentation and keyword-argument spacing rules
Use the Log keyword to output messages during test execution
Recognize the importance of whitespace in Robot Framework syntax

theory.title: Sequential Keyword Execution and Variable Assignment
theory.content:
## Test Cases as Workflows

Real-world test automation isn't just about executing a single action—it's about orchestrating **sequences of keywords** that represent complete user workflows or system interactions. Robot Framework executes keywords **sequentially from top to bottom**, making it intuitive to model step-by-step procedures.

### Multi-Step Test Structure

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
User Login Workflow
    Open Browser    https://example.com    Chrome
    Input Text      id:username          testuser
    Input Text      id:password          secret123
    Click Button    id:login-button
    Page Should Contain    Welcome, testuser!
```

Each line represents one action in the workflow. **Order matters**—you can't verify a welcome message before logging in!

## Variables in Robot Framework

Variables are containers for data that can be reused throughout your tests. The `Set Variable` keyword assigns a value to a variable at runtime.

### Variable Syntax

Robot Framework uses `${variable_name}` syntax for scalar variables:

```robot
${count}    Set Variable    10
${name}     Set Variable    John Doe
${result}   Set Variable    ${42}
```

**Important patterns:**
- Variable names are enclosed in `${...}`
- Assignment uses keyword `Set Variable`
- Variables appear **before** the keyword (return value position)
- Variables can store strings, numbers, objects, or any Python type

### How Variable Assignment Works

The syntax might look unusual if you're coming from traditional programming:

```robot
# Robot Framework syntax
${count}    Set Variable    10

# Similar to Python
count = set_variable(10)
```

In Robot Framework:
1. The leftmost column is the **return value** (variable receiving the result)
2. Next comes the **keyword name**
3. Then come **arguments** to the keyword

This pattern applies to **any keyword that returns a value**.

### Using Variables

Once assigned, variables can be used anywhere:

```robot
${count}    Set Variable    10
Log         Count is: ${count}
Log         ${count}
Should Be Equal    ${count}    10
```

Variables are **substituted** before keyword execution. When you write `Log    ${count}`, Robot Framework replaces `${count}` with its value (`10`) before calling the Log keyword.

## Why Sequential Execution Matters

### Readability and Maintainability

Sequential keyword execution makes tests read like **documentation**:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Place Order Test
    Log              Starting order workflow
    ${product_id}    Set Variable    12345
    Add To Cart      ${product_id}
    Proceed To Checkout
    ${total}         Get Order Total
    Log              Total: ${total}
    Confirm Order
```

Anyone reading this—technical or non-technical—can understand what the test does.

### Debugging and Logging

Using `Log` statements between actions helps track execution:

```robot
${result}    Calculate Value    5    10
Log          Intermediate result: ${result}
${final}     Multiply By Two    ${result}
Log          Final result: ${final}
```

Logs appear in `log.html`, creating a **traceable audit trail** of test execution.

## Best Practices

1. **One action per line:** Each keyword should do one clear thing
2. **Meaningful variable names:** `${user_count}` is better than `${x}`
3. **Log important values:** Helps debugging when tests fail
4. **Consistent indentation:** Always 4 spaces for readability

By mastering sequential keyword execution and variable usage, you can build complex test scenarios from simple, reusable building blocks.
learningObjectives: Execute multiple keywords sequentially in a single test case
Understand the order of execution in Robot Framework tests
Create and assign values to variables using Set Variable
Use variables in subsequent keywords within the same test

theory.title: Assertions and Verification in Robot Framework
theory.content:
## What Are Assertions?

In test automation, an **assertion** is a statement that verifies an expected condition is true. Assertions are the foundation of testing—they're how you actually **validate** that your system behaves correctly. Without assertions, you're just executing actions without verifying outcomes.

### The Role of Assertions

Consider a login test:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Login Test Without Assertion
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        user@example.com
    Input Text         id:password        secret
    Click Button       id:login
    # Test ends... but did login succeed? We don't know!
```

Versus:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Login Test With Assertion
    Open Browser            https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text              id:username        user@example.com
    Input Text              id:password        secret
    Click Button            id:login
    Page Should Contain     Welcome Dashboard  # ASSERTION!
```

The assertion **validates the expected outcome**, turning an action sequence into a real test.

## The Should Be Equal Keyword

`Should Be Equal` is one of the most fundamental assertion keywords in Robot Framework's BuiltIn library. It compares two values and **fails the test** if they don't match.

### Syntax

```robot
Should Be Equal    first    second
Should Be Equal    first    second    Custom error message
```

**Parameters:**
- `first`: First value to compare
- `second`: Second value to compare
- `msg`: Optional custom error message (shown on failure)

### How It Works

```robot
# Simple equality check
Should Be Equal    5    5                    # PASS
Should Be Equal    5    6                    # FAIL
Should Be Equal    Hello    Hello            # PASS
Should Be Equal    Hello    hello            # FAIL (case-sensitive)
```

When the assertion **fails**, Robot Framework:
1. Marks the test case as **FAIL**
2. Stops executing remaining keywords in that test
3. Shows a detailed error message in the log
4. Continues with the next test case (doesn't stop entire suite)

### Type Conversion

By default, `Should Be Equal` compares values as **strings**:

```robot
Should Be Equal    5      5         # PASS (both become "5")
Should Be Equal    5      ${5}      # PASS (number 5 becomes "5")
```

For strict type checking, use `Should Be Equal As Numbers` or `Should Be Equal As Integers`:

```robot
${num}    Set Variable    ${5}
Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${num}    5    # Strict numeric comparison
```

## Common Assertion Keywords

Robot Framework provides a rich set of assertion keywords:

### Equality Assertions
```robot
Should Be Equal              5    5
Should Not Be Equal          5    6
Should Be Equal As Numbers   5.0  5
Should Be Equal As Strings   5    5
```

### Comparison Assertions
```robot
Should Be Greater Than       10    5
Should Be Less Than          3     7
```

### Boolean Assertions
```robot
Should Be True     ${condition}
Should Be False    ${flag}
```

### Existence Assertions
```robot
Should Contain       Hello World    World
Should Not Contain   Hello World    Goodbye
```

## Why Start With Simple Assertions?

The `Should Be Equal    5    5` exercise might seem trivial, but it teaches critical concepts:

1. **Assertion syntax:** Understanding the pattern used by all assertion keywords
2. **Pass/fail mechanics:** How Robot Framework determines test success
3. **Verification mindset:** The importance of validating outcomes, not just executing actions
4. **Error handling:** What happens when assertions fail

### Building to Real Tests

Once you understand basic assertions, you can build realistic tests:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Calculator Test
    ${result}    Calculate Sum    2    3
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    5
    
    ${product}    Calculate Product    4    5
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${product}    20
```

Every real test follows this pattern:
1. **Arrange:** Set up test data and preconditions
2. **Act:** Perform the action being tested
3. **Assert:** Verify the expected outcome

Mastering assertions is mastering the "Assert" step—the most critical part of any test.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and importance of assertions in testing
Use the Should Be Equal keyword to verify expected values
Recognize how failed assertions affect test execution
Differentiate between test actions and test verifications

theory.title: Test Case Metadata: Documentation and Tags
theory.content:
## Why Document Test Cases?

As test suites grow from 10 tests to 100 or 1,000, **organization becomes critical**. Documentation and tags are Robot Framework's built-in mechanisms for making test suites maintainable, searchable, and understandable by teams.

### The Problem Without Documentation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
TC_001
    Login User    admin    password123
    Navigate To Settings
    Update Profile    New Name
    Logout
```

Questions arise:
- What does TC_001 actually test?
- Who wrote it and why?
- What's the expected behavior?
- When should this test run?

### The Solution: Built-In Metadata

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
User Profile Update Test
    [Documentation]    Verifies that authenticated users can update their profile name
    ...                Prerequisites: Valid user account exists
    ...                Expected: Profile changes are saved and displayed
    [Tags]    profile    settings    regression    smoke
    Login User         admin    password123
    Navigate To Settings
    Update Profile     New Name
    Logout
```

Now the test is **self-documenting** and **discoverable**.

## Documentation Setting

The `[Documentation]` setting provides a human-readable description of what the test does and why it exists.

### Syntax

```robot
[Documentation]    Single line description

# Multi-line documentation
[Documentation]    First line of description
...                Second line of description
...                Third line of description
```

**Key points:**
- Must come **immediately after** the test case name
- Uses 4-space indentation
- Multi-line docs use `...` continuation marker
- Appears in **reports and logs**
- Supports HTML formatting and links

### What to Include

Good documentation answers:
- **What:** What functionality is being tested?
- **Why:** Why is this test important?
- **How:** Any special setup or preconditions?
- **Expected:** What should happen?

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Password Complexity Validation
    [Documentation]    Tests that password must meet complexity requirements:
    ...                - Minimum 8 characters
    ...                - At least one uppercase letter
    ...                - At least one number
    ...                - At least one special character
    ...                Bug reference: ISSUE-1234
    [Tags]    security    validation    critical
```

## Tags: Organizing and Filtering Tests

Tags are **labels** you attach to test cases for organization, filtering, and selective execution.

### Syntax

```robot
[Tags]    tag1    tag2    tag3
```

**Characteristics:**
- Multiple tags separated by 4 spaces (or 2+)
- Case-insensitive when filtering
- Can be added at test or suite level
- Inherited from suite settings

### Common Tagging Strategies

#### By Test Type
```robot
[Tags]    smoke       # Quick critical tests
[Tags]    regression  # Comprehensive tests
[Tags]    integration # System integration tests
[Tags]    unit        # Component-level tests
```

#### By Feature/Module
```robot
[Tags]    login    authentication
[Tags]    checkout    payment
[Tags]    profile    user-management
```

#### By Priority/Severity
```robot
[Tags]    critical    blocker
[Tags]    high        priority-1
[Tags]    low         nice-to-have
```

#### By Execution Context
```robot
[Tags]    nightly     # Run in nightly builds
[Tags]    manual      # Requires manual intervention
[Tags]    wip         # Work in progress
```

### Selective Test Execution

Tags enable powerful filtering when running tests:

```bash
# Run only tests tagged 'smoke'
robot --include smoke tests/

# Run tests tagged 'login' OR 'logout'
robot --include loginORlogout tests/

# Run tests tagged 'regression' but NOT 'slow'
robot --include regression --exclude slow tests/

# Run tests with tag 'critical' AND 'api'
robot --include criticalANDapi tests/
```

This allows:
- **Fast smoke tests** before commits
- **Full regression** in CI/CD pipelines
- **Feature-specific testing** during development
- **Priority-based execution** when time-constrained

## Suite-Level Settings

You can also apply documentation and tags to entire suites:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Documentation    Test suite for user authentication features
...              Covers login, logout, password reset, and session management
Force Tags       authentication    regression
Default Tags     web-ui

*** Test Cases ***
Login Test
    [Tags]    smoke    # Inherits: authentication, regression, web-ui, smoke
    # Test implementation
```

- **Force Tags:** Applied to ALL tests in suite (can't be removed)
- **Default Tags:** Applied unless test overrides with its own tags

## Best Practices

### Documentation
1. **Be concise but complete:** 1-3 sentences usually sufficient
2. **Include bug IDs:** Link to issue tracker when relevant
3. **Document preconditions:** What must be true before test runs?
4. **Update when tests change:** Keep docs in sync with code

### Tags
1. **Use consistent naming:** Establish team conventions
2. **Avoid tag explosion:** Too many tags = no organization
3. **Combine strategies:** Use type + feature + priority
4. **Document tag meanings:** Create a tag dictionary for teams

### Example: Well-Organized Test

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Successful User Registration Flow
    [Documentation]    Verifies new users can register with valid email and password.
    ...                After registration, user receives confirmation email and
    ...                can log in with credentials.
    ...                Related: USER-STORY-456
    [Tags]    registration    smoke    high-priority    email
    Navigate To Registration Page
    Fill Registration Form    user@example.com    ValidPass123!
    Submit Registration
    Email Should Be Received    user@example.com    Welcome to App
    Login With Credentials      user@example.com    ValidPass123!
    Dashboard Should Be Visible
```

This test is:
- **Discoverable:** Easy to find via tags
- **Understandable:** Clear documentation explains purpose
- **Traceable:** Links to user story
- **Filterable:** Can run smoke tests or registration tests independently

Mastering documentation and tags transforms disorganized test suites into **structured, maintainable test assets**.
learningObjectives: Add documentation to test cases to explain their purpose and context
Use tags to categorize and organize tests for selective execution
Understand the syntax and placement of [Documentation] and [Tags] settings
Apply metadata best practices for maintainable test suites

theory.title: Organizing Multiple Test Cases in a Suite
theory.content:
## Test Suites: The Container for Test Cases

In Robot Framework, a **test suite** is a collection of test cases stored in a single `.robot` file (or directory). Each suite represents a logical grouping of related tests—for example, all tests for a specific feature, module, or user workflow.

### Why Multiple Test Cases Per Suite?

Real applications require **many test scenarios** to achieve adequate coverage:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Valid Login
    # Test successful login

Invalid Password
    # Test wrong password

Invalid Username
    # Test non-existent user

Locked Account
    # Test disabled account

Session Timeout
    # Test session expiration
```

Grouping related scenarios in one suite provides:
- **Logical organization:** All login tests in `login_tests.robot`
- **Shared setup/teardown:** Suite-level initialization
- **Better reporting:** Clear test categories in results
- **Easier maintenance:** Related tests in one place

## Syntax for Multiple Test Cases

Test cases within a suite are separated by **one or more blank lines**:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
First Test
    Log    This is test 1
    Should Be Equal    1    1

Second Test
    Log    This is test 2
    Should Be Equal    2    2

Third Test
    Log    This is test 3
    Should Be Equal    3    3
```

**Key rules:**
1. Each test case name starts at the **beginning of the line** (no indentation)
2. Test case steps are indented with **4 spaces**
3. Test cases are separated by **blank lines**
4. Order in file = execution order (by default)

## Independent Test Execution

Each test case is **independent** and **isolated**:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test One
    ${var}    Set Variable    100
    Log    ${var}

Test Two
    Log    ${var}    # FAIL! Variable from Test One doesn't exist here
```

**Important characteristics:**
- Each test starts with a **clean state**
- Variables don't carry over between tests (unless suite/global scope)
- One test's failure doesn't prevent others from running
- Tests can be executed individually or as a group

## The Evaluate Keyword

The `Evaluate` keyword executes Python expressions and returns the result, making it useful for calculations:

```robot
${sum}        Evaluate    2 + 3           # Returns 5
${product}    Evaluate    4 * 5           # Returns 20
${comparison} Evaluate    10 > 5          # Returns True
${length}     Evaluate    len('hello')    # Returns 5
```

### Common Uses

**Mathematical operations:**
```robot
${total}    Evaluate    ${price} * ${quantity}
${avg}      Evaluate    sum([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) / 5
```

**String operations:**
```robot
${upper}    Evaluate    'hello'.upper()          # HELLO
${joined}   Evaluate    '-'.join(['a','b','c'])  # a-b-c
```

**Conditional expressions:**
```robot
${status}    Evaluate    'pass' if ${score} >= 60 else 'fail'
```

**Type conversions:**
```robot
${num}    Evaluate    int('42')
${str}    Evaluate    str(123)
```

### Security Note

`Evaluate` executes **arbitrary Python code**, so use with caution:
- Prefer built-in keywords when available
- Don't evaluate untrusted user input
- For simple math, consider `Set Variable` with numeric operations

## Test Suite Execution Flow

When Robot Framework executes a suite:

```
1. Suite Setup (if defined)
   |
   v
2. Test Case 1
   - Test Setup (if defined)
   - Test steps
   - Test Teardown (if defined)
   |
   v
3. Test Case 2
   - Test Setup (if defined)
   - Test steps
   - Test Teardown (if defined)
   |
   v
4. Test Case N
   - Test Setup (if defined)
   - Test steps
   - Test Teardown (if defined)
   |
   v
5. Suite Teardown (if defined)
```

**Result aggregation:**
- Suite **PASSES** if all tests pass
- Suite **FAILS** if any test fails
- Individual test results shown in reports

## Best Practices for Test Organization

### 1. Logical Grouping

Group tests by feature or functionality:

```
login_tests.robot
    ├─ Valid Login
    ├─ Invalid Password
    └─ Account Lockout

profile_tests.robot
    ├─ View Profile
    ├─ Edit Profile
    └─ Delete Profile
```

### 2. Naming Conventions

Use descriptive, action-oriented names:

```robot
# Good names
User Can Login With Valid Credentials
System Rejects Invalid Email Format
Order Total Includes Tax And Shipping

# Poor names
Test1
TC_042
Check Thing
```

### 3. Suite Size

Balance granularity with manageability:
- **Too small:** 100 suites with 1-2 tests each (hard to navigate)
- **Too large:** 1 suite with 500 tests (slow, unwieldy)
- **Sweet spot:** 10-50 related tests per suite

### 4. Test Independence

Each test should be **runnable in isolation**:

```robot
# Bad: Tests depend on execution order
Test 1 - Create User
    Create User    testuser

Test 2 - Login As User
    Login    testuser    password    # Fails if Test 1 didn't run!

# Good: Each test is self-contained
Test 1 - Create User
    Create User    testuser
    User Should Exist    testuser
    [Teardown]    Delete User    testuser

Test 2 - Login As User
    Create User    testuser    password
    Login    testuser    password
    [Teardown]    Delete User    testuser
```

### 5. Clear Assertions

Every test should verify something specific:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Addition Test
    ${result}    Evaluate    2+2
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    4
    
Subtraction Test
    ${result}    Evaluate    5-3
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    2
```

Each test has:
- **One primary purpose:** Test addition or subtraction
- **Clear verification:** Explicit assertion
- **Obvious pass/fail:** No ambiguity

## Scaling to Larger Suites

As suites grow, consider:

**Setup and teardown:**
```robot
*** Settings ***
Suite Setup     Initialize Test Environment
Suite Teardown  Cleanup Test Environment
Test Setup      Reset To Default State
```

**Shared resources:**
```robot
*** Settings ***
Resource    ../resources/common_keywords.robot
Resource    ../resources/test_data.robot
```

**Data-driven testing:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Calculation Tests
    [Template]    Verify Calculation
    2+2    4
    5-3    2
    4*3    12
    10/2   5
```

By understanding how to organize multiple test cases effectively, you create **maintainable, scalable test suites** that grow with your application.
learningObjectives: Organize multiple related test cases within a single test suite
Understand test case independence and execution flow
Use the Evaluate keyword to perform calculations and Python expressions
Apply best practices for test naming and organization

theory.title: Comments and Code Documentation in Robot Framework
theory.content:
## The Purpose of Comments

Comments are **non-executable text** embedded in your code to explain **why** something is done, not just **what** is done. While Robot Framework's keyword-driven syntax is inherently readable, comments add context that code alone cannot convey.

### When Code Speaks for Itself

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
User Login Test
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        testuser
    Input Text         id:password        secret123
    Click Button       id:login
```

This code is self-explanatory—the keywords clearly describe actions.

### When Comments Add Value

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
User Login Test
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    
    # Using test user created in database migration v2.3
    Input Text         id:username        testuser
    Input Text         id:password        secret123
    
    Click Button       id:login
    
    # Bug #1234: Login button sometimes takes 2 clicks
    # Workaround: Wait 1 second before proceeding
    Sleep              1s
```

Now we understand **context**:
- Where test data comes from
- Why there's an unexpected wait
- Links to external references

## Comment Syntax

Robot Framework uses the hash symbol (`#`) for comments:

```robot
# This is a comment
    # This is an indented comment
```

### Placement Rules

**1. Start-of-line comments:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    # This comment describes the next action
    Log    Hello World
```

**2. Inline comments (after code):**
```robot
Log    Hello World    # This logs to console
```

**3. Indentation matches code:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    # Comment at test case level
    Log    First step
    # Comment at same level
    Log    Second step
```

### Multi-Line Comments

Robot Framework doesn't have block comment syntax. Use multiple single-line comments:

```robot
# This is a long explanation that spans
# multiple lines to describe complex logic
# that requires detailed documentation
${result}    Complex Keyword    arg1    arg2
```

## What to Comment (and What Not to)

### DO Comment:

**1. Complex logic or workarounds:**
```robot
# Workaround for ISSUE-456: API returns stale data
# Must clear cache before each request
Clear API Cache
${data}    Get User Data    user_id=123
```

**2. Business rules or requirements:**
```robot
# Per company policy: Users under 18 cannot create accounts
${age}    Get User Age    ${user_id}
Run Keyword If    ${age} < 18    Fail    User must be 18 or older
```

**3. External dependencies or data sources:**
```robot
# Test data from: configs/test_users.csv
# Maintained by QA team, updated weekly
${users}    Load Test Users From CSV
```

**4. Known issues or technical debt:**
```robot
# TODO: Replace with proper API once backend team finishes endpoint
# Tracking: BACKEND-789
${result}    Evaluate    {'status': 'mock_data'}
```

**5. Non-obvious timing or synchronization:**
```robot
# UI animation takes 500ms, wait for completion
Sleep    0.5s
Element Should Be Visible    id:welcome-message
```

### DON'T Comment:

**1. Obvious code:**
```robot
# Bad: Comment restates the code
# Log the message hello
Log    hello

# Good: No comment needed, code is clear
Log    hello
```

**2. Outdated information:**
```robot
# Bad: Comment contradicts code
# Set status to inactive
${status}    Set Variable    active    # Code was updated, comment wasn't!
```

**3. Commented-out code (usually):**
```robot
# Bad: Dead code clutters the file
# Log    This is old code
# ${old_var}    Set Variable    obsolete

# Good: Delete it or move to version control
```

Exception: Temporarily comment code during debugging, but clean up before committing.

## Comments vs. Documentation

Understand the difference:

### Comments (Internal)
- For **developers** maintaining the code
- Explain **implementation details**
- Not visible in test reports

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    # Using SHA-256 because MD5 is deprecated
    ${hash}    Generate Hash    SHA-256    ${data}
```

### Documentation (External)
- For **stakeholders** reading test reports
- Describe **what and why** at high level
- Visible in HTML reports and logs

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Password Hashing Test
    [Documentation]    Verifies that user passwords are hashed using SHA-256
    ...                before storage, as per security requirement SEC-42
    # Implementation uses SHA-256 because MD5 is deprecated
    ${hash}    Generate Hash    SHA-256    ${password}
```

## Comment Best Practices

### 1. Explain Why, Not What

```robot
# Poor: Repeats what the code does
# Set variable count to 10
${count}    Set Variable    10

# Good: Explains why this value
# API limit is 10 requests per batch
${count}    Set Variable    10
```

### 2. Keep Comments Updated

When code changes, update comments:

```robot
# Outdated after code change
# Retry 3 times before failing
Wait Until Keyword Succeeds    5x    1s    API Call

# Updated to match reality
# Retry 5 times before failing (increased for flaky API)
Wait Until Keyword Succeeds    5x    1s    API Call
```

### 3. Use TODO/FIXME/NOTE Markers

```robot
# TODO: Add validation for negative numbers
# FIXME: This fails on Windows, needs investigation
# NOTE: This timeout value is configurable in config.yaml
```

### 4. Link to External Resources

```robot
# Based on algorithm described in:
# https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luhn_algorithm
${is_valid}    Validate Credit Card Number    ${card_number}

# Reproduces bug reported in:
# https://jira.company.com/browse/BUG-1234
```

### 5. Section Dividers for Long Files

```robot
*** Test Cases ***

# ========================================
# Positive Test Cases
# ========================================

Successful Login
    ...

Successful Logout
    ...

# ========================================
# Negative Test Cases
# ========================================

Invalid Password
    ...
```

## Comments in Different Sections

### Settings Section
```robot
*** Settings ***
# Using custom library for PDF validation
Library    PdfLibrary

# Shared keywords for all login tests
Resource    login_keywords.robot

# Clean up users created during tests
Suite Teardown    Delete Test Users
```

### Variables Section
```robot
*** Variables ***
# Production API endpoint
${API_URL}    https://api.production.com

# Default timeout for all API calls (in seconds)
${TIMEOUT}    30

# Test data: user accounts from configs/users.json
${ADMIN_USER}    admin@example.com
```

### Keywords Section
```robot
*** Keywords ***
Login As User
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    # Using CSS selector because ID is dynamic
    Input Text    css:.username-field    ${username}
    Input Text    css:.password-field    ${password}
    Click Button    id:login-btn
```

## When Comments Indicate Deeper Issues

Sometimes excessive comments signal code that should be refactored:

```robot
# Poor: Comment explains confusing code
# This calculates the discounted price after applying
# the 15% loyalty discount and 10% seasonal discount
${price}    Evaluate    ${original_price} * 0.85 * 0.90

# Better: Extract to keyword with clear name
${price}    Calculate Price With Discounts    ${original_price}

*** Keywords ***
Calculate Price With Discounts
    [Arguments]    ${original_price}
    ${with_loyalty}    Evaluate    ${original_price} * 0.85
    ${final_price}     Evaluate    ${with_loyalty} * 0.90
    [Return]    ${final_price}
```

If you need many comments to explain code, consider:
- Breaking complex keywords into smaller steps
- Using more descriptive variable/keyword names
- Extracting magic numbers into named variables

Mastering comments means knowing **when to add context** and **when to let clear code speak for itself**.
learningObjectives: Use comments to add context and explanations to test code
Understand the difference between comments and documentation
Apply commenting best practices (explain why, not what)
Recognize when comments indicate need for refactoring

theory.title: Robot Framework Spacing and Indentation Rules
theory.content:
## Why Spacing Matters in Robot Framework

Unlike many programming languages that use parentheses, brackets, or explicit delimiters, Robot Framework uses **whitespace** as its primary syntax element. This design choice prioritizes **readability** but demands **strict adherence** to spacing conventions.

### The Whitespace-Based Syntax Philosophy

**Traditional languages:**
```python
login(username, password)  # Comma-separated arguments
```

**Robot Framework:**
```robot
Login    username    password    # Space-separated arguments
```

Robot Framework's whitespace syntax makes tests readable as **plain English**, but incorrect spacing causes:
- **Syntax errors:** Keywords not recognized
- **Argument confusion:** Values merged or split incorrectly  
- **Execution failures:** Tests behave unexpectedly
- **Maintenance nightmares:** Inconsistent formatting across files

## The Two Critical Spacing Rules

### Rule 1: Indentation (4 Spaces)

All content **within** a section must be indented with **exactly 4 spaces**:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test Name           # No indentation (test case name)
    Log    Message    # 4-space indentation (test case content)
    Should Be Equal    1    1    # 4-space indentation

*** Keywords ***
My Keyword             # No indentation (keyword name)
    [Arguments]    ${arg}    # 4-space indentation (keyword content)
    Log    ${arg}            # 4-space indentation
```

**Common mistakes:**
```robot
# Wrong: 2 spaces
  Log    Message

# Wrong: 6 spaces
      Log    Message

# Wrong: Tab character (may look like 4 spaces but isn't)
	Log    Message

# Correct: Exactly 4 spaces
    Log    Message
```

### Rule 2: Keyword-Argument Separation (4+ Spaces)

Keywords and arguments must be separated by **at least 4 spaces** (recommended) or **2+ spaces** (minimum):

```robot
# Recommended: 4 spaces between keyword and arguments
Log    Hello World
Should Be Equal    5    5

# Also valid: More than 4 spaces (for alignment)
Log              Hello World
Should Be Equal  5    5

# Minimum valid: 2 spaces (but discouraged)
Log  Hello World
```

**Arguments separated by 4+ spaces:**
```robot
Keyword    arg1    arg2    arg3
```

## Data Format Detection

Robot Framework supports multiple data formats, but **space-separated** is most common:

### Space Format (Standard)
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    Log    Message    # 4 spaces = separator
```

### Tab Format (Alternative)
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
	Log	Message    # Tabs = separator
```

### Pipe Format (Explicit)
```robot
| *** Test Cases *** |
| My Test            |
|     | Log | Message |
```

**Recommendation:** Use **space format** with 4-space separators—it's the most widely adopted convention.

## Common Spacing Errors and Fixes

### Error 1: Inconsistent Indentation

```robot
# Bad: Mixed indentation
*** Test Cases ***
Badly Formatted Test
  Log    Hello      # 2 spaces - WRONG
      Log    World  # 6 spaces - WRONG
    Log    Test     # 4 spaces - CORRECT

# Good: Consistent 4-space indentation
*** Test Cases ***
Properly Formatted Test
    Log    Hello    # 4 spaces
    Log    World    # 4 spaces
    Log    Test     # 4 spaces
```

**Result of inconsistent indentation:**
- Robot Framework may interpret lines as continuations
- Keywords may not execute
- Arguments may be misinterpreted

### Error 2: Insufficient Keyword-Argument Spacing

```robot
# Bad: Only 1 space
Log Message

# Bad: Only 2 spaces (minimum, but discouraged)
Log  Message

# Good: 4 spaces (standard)
Log    Message
```

**Why 4 spaces is preferred:**
- **Consistency:** Same as indentation rule
- **Clarity:** Visually distinct keyword vs. arguments
- **Alignment:** Easier to align arguments in columnar style

### Error 3: Tabs vs. Spaces

```robot
# Invisible error: Looks correct but uses tabs
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
	Log    Message    # Tab character - may cause issues

# Correct: Actual spaces
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    Log    Message    # 4 space characters
```

**Editor configuration:**
Most editors can show whitespace characters to detect tabs. Configure your editor to:
- Convert tabs to spaces automatically
- Use 4 spaces per tab
- Show invisible characters when needed

### Error 4: Trailing Whitespace

```robot
# Can cause subtle issues
Log    Message    
               ^^^^ trailing spaces may cause parsing errors

# Clean
Log    Message
```

## Tools for Maintaining Proper Spacing

### Robot Framework IDE (RIDE)
- Automatically formats spacing
- Validates syntax in real-time
- Highlights spacing errors

### Robotidy (Auto-formatter)
```bash
pip install robotframework-tidy
robotidy tests/    # Auto-fix spacing in all test files
```

### VS Code Extensions
- **Robot Framework Language Server:** Syntax validation
- **EditorConfig:** Enforce 4-space indentation

### .editorconfig Example
```ini
[*.robot]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
insert_final_newline = true
```

## Visual Spacing Guide

Use invisible character markers to see spacing:

```
***·Test·Cases·***
My·Test·Name
····Log····Hello·World
····Should·Be·Equal····5····5

^ = start of line
· = space character
```

**Breakdown:**
- Test name: No leading spaces
- Keywords: 4 leading spaces
- Keyword-argument gap: 4 spaces
- Argument-argument gap: 4 spaces

## Style Guide Recommendations

### Indentation
- **Always 4 spaces** for test case and keyword content
- **Never use tabs** (configure editor to convert)
- **Be consistent** throughout entire project

### Keyword-Argument Spacing
- **Minimum:** 4 spaces (recommended standard)
- **Alignment:** Optionally align arguments for readability

```robot
# Minimal spacing (valid)
Log                     Message
Should Be Equal         5         5

# Aligned spacing (more readable in some cases)
Log                     Message
Should Be Equal         5                5
```

### Section Headers
```robot
# Correct: Three asterisks, spaces, name, three asterisks
*** Settings ***
*** Variables ***
*** Test Cases ***
*** Keywords ***

# Wrong: Inconsistent spacing
***Settings***
*** Variables***
***  Test Cases  ***
```

## Debugging Spacing Issues

When tests fail with cryptic errors:

1. **Check indentation:** Ensure exactly 4 spaces
2. **Check separators:** Ensure 4+ spaces between elements
3. **Check for tabs:** Convert all tabs to spaces
4. **Check trailing whitespace:** Remove extra spaces at line ends
5. **Use formatters:** Run `robotidy` or IDE auto-format

### Example Debugging

```robot
# Error: "Keyword 'Log    Hello' not found"
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
  Log    Hello    # Only 2-space indentation!

# Fixed
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    Log    Hello    # Correct 4-space indentation
```

## Why This Exercise Matters

The "Fix Spacing and Indentation" exercise teaches:

1. **Attention to detail:** Whitespace is syntax in Robot Framework
2. **Debugging skills:** Identifying and fixing formatting errors
3. **Best practices:** Learning standard conventions early
4. **Tool configuration:** Setting up editors correctly

Mastering spacing rules **prevents countless hours** of debugging mysterious test failures caused by invisible characters and inconsistent formatting.

## Quick Reference

```robot
*** Section Name ***     # Sections: *** Name ***
Test/Keyword Name        # Names: No indentation
    Keyword    arg1    arg2    # Content: 4 spaces indent, 4 spaces separator
    [Setting]    value          # Settings: 4 spaces indent, 4 spaces separator
```

**Golden rules:**
1. Indent with **4 spaces** (not tabs, not 2, not 6)
2. Separate with **4 spaces** (keyword from args, arg from arg)
3. Be **consistent** across all files
4. Use **tools** to automate formatting

Proper spacing isn't just about making tests work—it's about making them **maintainable, professional, and reliable**.
learningObjectives: Understand Robot Framework's whitespace-based syntax rules
Apply the 4-space indentation rule consistently
Use 4-space separation between keywords and arguments
Identify and fix common spacing and indentation errors
relatedConcepts: Data format detection (space, tab, pipe formats)

theory.title: Complete Robot Framework Suite Structure and Sections
theory.content:
## Anatomy of a Robot Framework File

A Robot Framework file (`.robot`) is a **self-contained test suite** organized into distinct **sections**. Each section serves a specific purpose, and understanding their roles and relationships is fundamental to writing professional, maintainable test automation.

### The Four Core Sections

```robot
*** Settings ***
# Configuration: libraries, resources, setup/teardown

*** Variables ***
# Test data and constants

*** Test Cases ***
# The actual test scenarios

*** Keywords ***
# Custom reusable keywords (functions)
```

**Key principles:**
- Sections are **optional** (only include what you need)
- Section **order is recommended** but not strictly enforced (except Test Cases before Keywords is common)
- Sections make large files **organized and scannable**

## Settings Section

The `*** Settings ***` section configures how the suite operates.

### Common Settings

**Library imports:**
```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    SeleniumLibrary
Library    RequestsLibrary
Library    Collections
Library    CustomLibrary    arg1    arg2    # With arguments
```

**Resource imports:**
```robot
Resource    ../resources/common_keywords.robot
Resource    ../resources/test_data.robot
```

**Suite lifecycle:**
```robot
Suite Setup       Initialize Test Environment
Suite Teardown    Cleanup Test Environment
```

**Test lifecycle:**
```robot
Test Setup        Login As Test User
Test Teardown     Logout And Clear Session
```

**Metadata and documentation:**
```robot
Documentation     This suite tests the user management module
Metadata          Version    2.0
Metadata          Author     QA Team
```

**Test organization:**
```robot
Force Tags        regression    api
Default Tags      user-management
```

### Suite Setup and Teardown

**Suite Setup** runs **once** before all tests in the suite:
```robot
Suite Setup    Log    Suite Started
```

Common uses:
- Initialize database connections
- Start application servers
- Load configuration files
- Create test data

**Suite Teardown** runs **once** after all tests complete:
```robot
Suite Teardown    Close All Browsers
```

Common uses:
- Close database connections
- Delete temporary test data
- Archive logs
- Send notifications

**Execution flow:**
```
Suite Setup
  |
  v
Test 1 (with Test Setup/Teardown)
  |
  v
Test 2 (with Test Setup/Teardown)
  |
  v
Test N (with Test Setup/Teardown)
  |
  v
Suite Teardown
```

## Variables Section

The `*** Variables ***` section defines **test data** and **constants** available throughout the suite.

### Scalar Variables
```robot
*** Variables ***
${APP_NAME}        MyApp
${BASE_URL}        https://example.com
${TIMEOUT}         30
${ADMIN_USER}      admin@example.com
```

Usage:
```robot
Log    Application: ${APP_NAME}
Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
```

### List Variables
```robot
@{USERS}           alice    bob    charlie
@{BROWSERS}        Chrome   Firefox   Edge
```

Usage:
```robot
Log Many    @{USERS}           # Logs: alice, bob, charlie
FOR    ${user}    IN    @{USERS}
    Create Account    ${user}
END
```

### Dictionary Variables
```robot
&{ADMIN}           username=admin    password=secret123    role=admin
&{CONFIG}          api_key=abc123    timeout=30
```

Usage:
```robot
Log    ${ADMIN.username}      # Logs: admin
Login    ${ADMIN.username}    ${ADMIN.password}
```

### Variable Scope

Variables in `*** Variables ***` section have **suite scope**—available to:
- All test cases in the suite
- All keywords in the suite
- Imported resource files (that reference them)

### Variable Files

For complex data, use Python/YAML variable files:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Variables    configs/test_data.py
Variables    configs/environment.yaml
```

## Test Cases Section

The `*** Test Cases ***` section contains the actual test scenarios—this is the **heart** of your suite.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test App Name
    Log    ${APP_NAME}
    Should Be Equal    ${APP_NAME}    MyApp

Test Navigation
    Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
    Page Should Contain    Welcome
    [Teardown]    Close Browser
```

**Characteristics:**
- Each test is independent (can run in isolation)
- Tests execute sequentially (top to bottom)
- One failing test doesn't prevent others from running
- Test names should be descriptive and action-oriented

## Keywords Section

The `*** Keywords ***` section defines **custom keywords**—reusable functions that encapsulate common operations.

### Basic Custom Keyword

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Custom Keyword
    Log    Custom
```

Usage in tests:
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Custom Keyword
    Custom Keyword    # Calls your custom keyword
```

### Keywords with Arguments

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Login As User
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    Input Text     id:username    ${username}
    Input Text     id:password    ${password}
    Click Button   id:login
```

Usage:
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Login
    Login As User    testuser    secret123
```

### Keywords with Return Values

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Get Full Name
    [Arguments]    ${first}    ${last}
    ${full_name}    Set Variable    ${first} ${last}
    [Return]    ${full_name}
```

Usage:
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Name Concatenation
    ${name}    Get Full Name    John    Doe
    Should Be Equal    ${name}    John Doe
```

### Why Custom Keywords?

**Without custom keywords:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        user1
    Input Text         id:password        pass1
    Click Button       id:login
    Page Should Contain    Dashboard
    Close Browser

Test 2
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        user2
    Input Text         id:password        pass2
    Click Button       id:login
    Page Should Contain    Dashboard
    Close Browser
```

**With custom keywords:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    Login As User    user1    pass1
    Dashboard Should Be Visible

Test 2
    Login As User    user2    pass2
    Dashboard Should Be Visible

*** Keywords ***
Login As User
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        ${username}
    Input Text         id:password        ${password}
    Click Button       id:login
    [Teardown]         Close Browser

Dashboard Should Be Visible
    Page Should Contain    Dashboard
```

Benefits:
- **DRY principle:** Don't repeat yourself
- **Abstraction:** Hide implementation details
- **Maintainability:** Change once, fix everywhere
- **Readability:** Tests read like documentation

## Complete Suite Example

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library           SeleniumLibrary
Resource          ../resources/common.robot
Suite Setup       Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
Suite Teardown    Close All Browsers
Test Setup        Go To    ${BASE_URL}
Test Tags         web-ui    smoke

*** Variables ***
${BASE_URL}       https://example.com
${ADMIN_USER}     admin@example.com
${ADMIN_PASS}     secret123

*** Test Cases ***
Successful Login
    [Documentation]    Verifies admin can log in successfully
    [Tags]    login    critical
    Login As User    ${ADMIN_USER}    ${ADMIN_PASS}
    Dashboard Should Be Visible

Unsuccessful Login
    [Documentation]    Verifies system rejects invalid credentials
    [Tags]    login    security
    Login As User    invalid@example.com    wrongpass
    Error Message Should Be Displayed    Invalid credentials

*** Keywords ***
Login As User
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    Input Text     id:username    ${username}
    Input Text     id:password    ${password}
    Click Button   id:login-btn

Dashboard Should Be Visible
    Wait Until Page Contains    Dashboard    timeout=5s
    Location Should Be    ${BASE_URL}/dashboard

Error Message Should Be Displayed
    [Arguments]    ${message}
    Wait Until Page Contains    ${message}    timeout=3s
```

## Section Best Practices

### Settings
- Import only libraries you actually use
- Use Suite Setup for expensive one-time operations
- Use Test Setup for operations needed before EVERY test
- Add documentation for complex suites

### Variables
- Use UPPERCASE for constants: `${BASE_URL}`
- Use descriptive names: `${ADMIN_USER}` not `${U1}`
- Group related variables together
- Consider variable files for large datasets

### Test Cases
- One test = one scenario/workflow
- Descriptive names (not TC_001)
- Add [Documentation] for complex tests
- Use [Tags] for organization
- Keep tests focused and independent

### Keywords
- Create keywords for repeated operations (3+ uses)
- Use verb-based names: `Login As User`, `Verify Dashboard`
- Document complex keywords
- Keep keywords focused (single responsibility)

## When to Split Suites

One file is appropriate when:
- 10-50 related test cases
- All tests use same setup/teardown
- Tests belong to same feature/module

Split into multiple files when:
- Tests exceed 100+ cases
- Different tests need different setup
- Testing unrelated features
- File becomes hard to navigate

### Directory Structure for Multiple Suites

```
tests/
├── login_tests.robot
├── profile_tests.robot
├── checkout_tests.robot
└── resources/
    ├── common_keywords.robot
    ├── test_data.robot
    └── page_objects.robot
```

By mastering the complete suite structure, you create **organized, maintainable, and professional** test automation that scales from simple smoke tests to comprehensive test suites with thousands of test cases.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and structure of all four Robot Framework sections
Create a complete test suite with Settings, Variables, Test Cases, and Keywords
Use Suite Setup to perform one-time initialization before tests
Define custom keywords to encapsulate reusable test logic
